title: Micah 3:1–12
context: Micah addresses the heads of Jacob and rulers of Israel, who should know justice but hate the good and devour the people (3:1–4). The LORD speaks against prophets who cry “Peace!” for pay, promising them darkness and silence (3:5–7), while Micah declares that he is filled with power by the LORD’s Spirit to declare Israel’s sin (3:8). Rulers, priests, and prophets who work for bribes yet claim the LORD’s presence will see Zion plowed like a field (3:9–12). Jeremiah 26:18 quotes 3:12, recalling Micah in the days of Hezekiah.

verses.text: I said, “Please listen, you heads of Jacob, and rulers of the house of Israel: Isn’t it for you to know justice?
verses.arminianNotes: Micah says, “Please listen, you heads of Jacob, and rulers of the house of Israel: Isn’t it for you to know justice?” Arminian readers see leaders held responsible for knowing and doing justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see rulers accountable to God for justice. Shared ground: authority is a trust from God, and those who hold it must answer for how they use it.

verses.text: You who hate the good, and love the evil; who tear off their skin, and their flesh from off their bones;
verses.arminianNotes: “You who hate the good, and love the evil.” Arminian readers see moral inversion in the leaders, whose love and hatred are turned the wrong way, with violent imagery for their oppression.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see corrupt desires behind corrupt rule. The image of tearing skin is figurative for exploiting the people, and readers in this tradition read it soberly.

verses.text: who also eat the flesh of my people, and peel their skin from off them, and break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as meat within the cauldron.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse pictures the rulers devouring the people like meat for the pot. Arminian readers see a shocking metaphor for exploitation, meant to expose how the leaders treat those in their care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a vivid figure for oppression, read soberly. Shared ground: the prophet uses strong language so that injustice is seen for what it is, not to sensationalize violence.

verses.text: Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them. Yes, he will hide his face from them at that time, because they made their deeds evil.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them.” Arminian readers see prayer without repentance left unanswered, as the LORD hides his face from those who did evil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD withholding his answer from unrepentant oppressors. On whether prayer changes what God does, readers may consult the existing Joshua 10:14 box rather than a new discussion here.

verses.text: The LORD says concerning the prophets who lead my people astray—for those who feed their teeth, they proclaim, “Peace!” and whoever doesn’t provide for their mouths, they prepare war against him:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks against prophets who proclaim “Peace!” to those who feed them and war against those who do not. Arminian readers see prophecy corrupted by self-interest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see prophets selling their message. Shared ground: readers in both traditions commonly hear a warning against ministry shaped by payment rather than by faithfulness to God’s word.

verses.text: “Therefore night is over you, with no vision, and it is dark to you, that you may not divine; and the sun will go down on the prophets, and the day will be black over them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore night is over you, with no vision.” Arminian readers see false prophets left in darkness, their supposed insight taken away as judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD removing vision from those who misused it. Readers in this tradition note the fitting judgment: those who sold visions will have none.

verses.text: The seers shall be disappointed, and the diviners confounded. Yes, they shall all cover their lips, for there is no answer from God.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The seers shall be disappointed, and the diviners confounded.” and “there is no answer from God.” Arminian readers see false seers put to shame when God gives no word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the silence of God as judgment on false prophecy. Readers in this tradition note that covering the lips was a sign of shame and mourning.

verses.text: But as for me, I am full of power by the LORD’s Spirit, and of judgment, and of might, to declare to Jacob his disobedience, and to Israel his sin.
verses.arminianNotes: “But as for me, I am full of power by the LORD’s Spirit.” Arminian readers see Micah’s confidence resting on the Spirit who empowers him to declare Israel’s sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Spirit as the source of true prophetic power. Shared ground: faithful ministry depends on God’s Spirit and is willing to name sin plainly rather than offer false peace.

verses.text: Please listen to this, you heads of the house of Jacob, and rulers of the house of Israel, who abhor justice, and pervert all equity,
verses.arminianNotes: “Please listen to this, you heads of the house of Jacob,” and “who abhor justice, and pervert all equity”. Arminian readers see Micah repeating his call to the rulers with greater force.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the rulers charged with hating justice. Readers in this tradition note that the charge prepares for the sentence on Zion in 3:12.

verses.text: who build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: “who build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity.” Arminian readers see a city built through violence and injustice, whatever its outward splendor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see corruption at the foundations of Jerusalem. Shared ground: building projects and prosperity cannot excuse injustice, and God judges how a city is built as well as what it builds.

verses.text: Her leaders judge for bribes, and her priests teach for a price, and her prophets tell fortunes for money; yet they lean on the LORD, and say, “Isn’t the LORD among us? No disaster will come on us.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Her leaders judge for bribes, and her priests teach for a price.” Yet they say, “Isn’t the LORD among us?” Arminian readers see false confidence in God’s presence despite corruption.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see presumption: leaders claim the LORD’s protection while betraying his ways. Readers in this tradition note the same danger in Jeremiah 7:4, cited by reference.

verses.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field.” Jeremiah 26:18 quotes this verse, recalling Micah in Hezekiah’s days. Arminian readers note that Hezekiah’s response led the LORD to relent (Jeremiah 26:19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the quotation in Jeremiah 26:18–19. On the LORD relenting, readers may consult the existing 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10 boxes rather than a new discussion here.
